about: Overview

Licensing law decides who can sell alcohol, put on entertainment, serve hot food late at night or carry passengers for hire. In England and Wales most of this work is handled by local councils acting as licensing authorities. For pubs, bars, restaurants, shops, clubs and venues the main law is the Licensing Act 2003. For taxis and private hire vehicles it is a separate set of older laws, along with each council's own policy.

These permissions matter because trading without the right licence, or breaking the conditions on one, can be a criminal offence. A licence can also be one of the most valuable things a hospitality business owns. A bar with a late licence in a busy town centre is worth far more than the same building without one, and a taxi driver without a badge cannot earn a living.

Licensing is a specialist field. The procedures are detailed, the deadlines are strict and a lot depends on local policy and on the relationship between the business and bodies such as the police and environmental health. Many people only ever deal with it once or twice, which is why they often look for a solicitor who handles licensing work every day.

Every decision under the Licensing Act 2003 is made by reference to four licensing objectives. These are the prevention of crime and disorder, public safety, the prevention of public nuisance and the protection of children from harm. Councils, the police and residents have to tie any objection to one or more of these, and the council has to make its decision with them in mind.

Understanding the objectives is the key to most licensing work. A well prepared application shows how the business will promote each of them. A strong response to an objection shows why the concern raised either does not relate to the objectives or can be dealt with by sensible conditions.

Councils are expected to aim to permit licensable activities where they can, while promoting the objectives. In practice that means most applications are granted, often with conditions, and refusal or revocation is usually kept for cases where conditions would not be enough. That does not mean any particular application will succeed, and local policy can make a big difference.

What we cover
Licensing work falls into a handful of main types. Each has its own page on this site with more detail, but here is a short guide to help you work out which one fits.

A premises licence lets a particular place carry on licensable activities such as selling alcohol, providing regulated entertainment or serving hot food and drink between 11pm and 5am. A new application is needed for a new venue, or for existing premises that have never been licensed or whose licence has lapsed. It involves an operating schedule, a plan of the premises, public notices and a consultation period.

Once a premises has a licence, changes to hours, layout, activities or conditions usually need a variation. Some small changes can go through a simpler minor variation process. Larger changes follow a process much like a new application.

When a business is sold or the operator changes, the premises licence usually has to be transferred to the new holder. When the manager named as designated premises supervisor leaves, a new one has to be put in place. These are routine applications, but timing matters, especially on the sale of a business.

A review is where the police, another responsible authority or a member of the public asks the council to look again at a licence because of problems linked to the licensing objectives. The council can do anything from taking no action to revoking the licence. Reviews are often the most serious and urgent kind of licensing matter.

A personal licence is held by an individual and allows them to authorise the sale of alcohol from licensed premises. Questions often arise where the applicant has a criminal conviction, or where a holder is convicted and the council considers suspending or revoking the licence.

Drivers, vehicles and operators are licensed by the local council, or by Transport for London in London. Councils can refuse, suspend or revoke licences, sometimes with immediate effect, and drivers often need help quickly to protect their income.
Choosing a firm

Most general high street firms do not offer licensing work, so it helps to find a firm that does it regularly. Licensing law is closely tied to local practice. Every council has its own statement of licensing policy, and some areas have special policies for busy nightlife districts. A firm that knows how licensing committees work, and how the police licensing teams approach things, can make a real difference to how smoothly a matter goes.

about: It is also worth thinking about how the firm communicates. Licensing work often involves short notice requests from the police or council, so you want a firm that replies quickly and explains things in plain terms. For multi site operators, ask whether the firm can handle licences across different councils and keep track of renewals, annual fees and DPS changes for you.

Some licensing solicitors also work with licensing consultants, acoustic experts, security advisers or architects who draw licensing plans. For bigger applications or reviews, the firm may suggest using one of these specialists. Ask what they think is needed and what it would cost before you agree.

Licensing is not a reserved legal activity, so some help is offered by non-lawyer consultants. Leaflegal only introduces regulated law firms. A solicitor is regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority, carries insurance and is bound by rules on conduct and confidentiality. They can also represent you in the magistrates' court if a matter goes to appeal.

Licensing often overlaps with other areas. A business sale may involve commercial property and company work. A planning issue may sit alongside a licensing application. A taxi driver facing a licensing hearing may also have a related criminal matter, which needs a separate criminal defence firm. The licensing firm can tell you if any of these apply.
Do not worry if you are not sure what kind of help you need. Describe the problem in your own words on the form and the firm will work out which process applies.
Costs
Licensing costs come in two parts. There are the fees charged by the council, and there are the fees charged by the solicitor if you choose to use one.

Premises licence fees under the Licensing Act 2003 are set nationally and usually depend on the rateable value of the premises. There is an application fee and, once granted, an annual fee. Variations, transfers, DPS changes and personal licence applications each have their own fee. Taxi and private hire fees are set locally by each council and can vary a great deal between areas. Fees change from time to time, so check the current figures with your council or on GOV.UK.

Many licensing firms offer fixed fees for routine applications such as transfers, DPS changes, minor variations and straightforward new premises licences. Work that depends on how others respond, such as contested applications, reviews and appeals, is often charged on an hourly basis or as a staged fee, with a separate fee for attending a hearing.

Ask the firm what is included. For example, does the fee cover drafting the operating schedule, arranging the newspaper notice, talking to the police and attending a hearing if one is needed? Are council fees, plan drawing and advertising costs included or extra? A good firm will confirm its fees in writing before work starts.

For businesses with several sites, some firms offer retainers or annual packages covering routine changes and compliance checks. These can be more predictable than paying for each piece of work separately, but compare what is included with what you are likely to need.

Timescales
Licensing has fixed periods set by law, and councils have to follow them. This means some parts of the process cannot be rushed, however urgent your opening date is.

New premises licence applications and full variations have a consultation period during which responsible authorities and members of the public can make representations. If none are made, the licence is usually granted shortly afterwards. If representations are made and cannot be resolved, a hearing is arranged, which adds several weeks.

Temporary event notices have their own deadlines, measured in working days before the event. A late notice gives less time but is limited in number and can be stopped outright by a police or environmental health objection. If an event date is fixed, it is worth checking the deadlines well in advance.

Minor variations, transfers and DPS changes are usually quicker. Transfers and DPS changes can often be given immediate effect on application, so trading can continue while the council processes them.

Reviews follow a set timetable that leads to a hearing. Summary reviews brought by the police after serious crime or disorder move much faster, with interim steps considered within days. Taxi licence suspensions can take effect immediately in some cases.

Most licensing decisions can be appealed to the magistrates' court, but the time limit is short. In many cases it is 21 days from being told of the decision. If you think you may want to appeal, speak to a solicitor as soon as you receive the decision.
Councils differ in how quickly they process paperwork and list hearings. A local licensing firm will usually know what to expect in your area.

The biggest cause of delay is usually a problem with the paperwork, such as a plan that does not meet the requirements, a notice that was not displayed for the full period or a newspaper advert placed late. If any of these go wrong, the application may have to start again, which resets the clock. Building in some spare time before an opening date is sensible.
What to prepare

Getting organised before you speak to a firm will save time and can reduce costs. You do not need everything, but the more the solicitor can see at the start, the better they can explain where you stand.

It also helps to think about what really matters to you. For a new venue, is it the closing time, the right to have live music or permission for an outdoor area? For a review, is it keeping the licence at any cost or protecting particular hours? Knowing your priorities helps the solicitor focus on what counts.

faqs: About licensing
What is a licensable activity?

Under the Licensing Act 2003 the main licensable activities are selling alcohol by retail, supplying alcohol in a members club, providing regulated entertainment and providing late night refreshment, which is hot food or hot drink between 11pm and 5am. Some entertainment has been deregulated in certain circumstances, so not every event needs a licence. A licensing solicitor can explain how the rules apply to what you plan to do.
Who is the licensing authority?

For premises and personal licences, the licensing authority is usually the local district, borough, city or unitary council where the premises is, or where the applicant lives for a personal licence. For taxis and private hire, it is the council that issues the licence, or Transport for London for London. Each authority publishes its own licensing policy, which it must take into account when making decisions.
What are responsible authorities?

These are the public bodies that receive copies of premises licence applications and can make representations. They usually include the police, the fire and rescue authority, environmental health, planning, trading standards, the body responsible for child protection, the public health team, the licensing authority itself and Home Office Immigration Enforcement. Any of them can also apply for a review.
What is a statement of licensing policy?

Every licensing authority must publish a statement of its licensing policy and review it regularly. The policy explains how the council approaches applications, what it expects from operators and any local issues, such as areas with special rules on cumulative impact. Your solicitor will look at the relevant policy when preparing an application or responding to an objection.
Is planning permission the same as a licence?

No. Planning permission and licensing are separate regimes. A premises can hold a licence that allows later hours than the planning permission, or the other way round. Both usually need to be in place, and breaching either can cause problems. A solicitor can explain how the two interact for your premises and whether planning advice is also needed.
Does licensing cover gambling?

Gambling premises are licensed under a separate law, the Gambling Act 2005, with councils and the Gambling Commission both involved. Some licensing firms also handle gambling work. If your matter involves gaming machines in a pub or a betting or bingo premises, mention it on the form so the firm knows what you need.
Do I need a licence to play background music?

Not always. Recorded music and some live music in licensed premises have been deregulated within certain hours and audience sizes, and background music is generally not regulated entertainment. Separate copyright licences for playing music are a different matter and are not covered by the Licensing Act. A licensing solicitor can check whether your plans need to be on your premises licence.
Premises and people
What is a designated premises supervisor?

Premises licensed to sell alcohol usually need to name a designated premises supervisor, often called the DPS. This person must hold a personal licence and is usually the manager responsible for day to day running. The police see the DPS as their main point of contact. Some community premises can apply to remove this requirement.
Do all staff need a personal licence?

No. Every sale of alcohol must be made or authorised by a personal licence holder, but staff do not each need their own licence. In practice this means a personal licence holder, usually the DPS, authorises others to make sales. Many operators keep written authorisations and train staff on age checks and refusing sales.
What are licence conditions?

Conditions are the rules attached to a premises licence. Some are mandatory and apply to all alcohol licences, such as having an age verification policy. Others come from your own operating schedule or are added by the council, such as door staff at certain times or limits on outside drinking. Breaching a condition can be a criminal offence.
What is a temporary event notice?

A temporary event notice lets someone carry on licensable activities for a short event without a premises licence, subject to limits on numbers, length and how many notices can be given. It is given to the council and the police, who can object. There are standard and late notices with different deadlines. A solicitor can check whether a notice suits your plans.
Can I run a venue as a members club?

Genuine members clubs can apply for a club premises certificate instead of a premises licence. The club has to meet certain conditions about membership and how it is run. The rules are quite specific, so it is worth checking with a solicitor whether your organisation qualifies and which option suits it best.
What happens if a premises licence lapses?

A licence can lapse in some situations, such as the death, incapacity or insolvency of the holder. There are short time limits for steps that can keep it alive, such as an interim authority notice or a transfer. If you think a licence has lapsed or is about to, speak to a licensing solicitor quickly.
Problems and hearings
What is a licensing hearing?

A hearing takes place before a licensing sub-committee, usually three councillors, when an application or review cannot be agreed. The applicant, the responsible authorities and anyone who made representations can speak. Hearings are less formal than court, but they follow set rules. Many people choose to have a solicitor speak for them.
Can residents object to my licence?

Yes. Anyone can make a representation about a new application, a full variation or a review, as long as it relates to the licensing objectives and is not frivolous or vexatious. Representations are often about noise, anti-social behaviour or litter. A solicitor may be able to resolve concerns by agreeing conditions before a hearing.
What can the council do at a review?

At a review the council can take no action, issue a warning, change the conditions, remove a licensable activity, remove the designated premises supervisor, suspend the licence for up to three months or revoke it. The decision must be appropriate to promote the licensing objectives. Most decisions do not take effect until the appeal period ends.
Can I appeal a licensing decision?

Most licensing decisions can be appealed to the magistrates' court. The time limit is short, often 21 days from being told of the decision. The court looks at the matter again and can make a different decision. Appeals carry a risk of paying the other side's costs, so a solicitor will explain the risks before you decide.
What if the police close my premises?

The police and councils have powers to close premises quickly in some situations, such as serious disorder or nuisance, using closure notices and orders. A closure order can also lead to a licence review. These matters move very fast and often involve a court hearing within days. Contact a licensing solicitor as soon as possible.
Can I be prosecuted for licensing offences?

Yes. Offences include carrying on licensable activities without authorisation, breaching conditions, selling alcohol to children and allowing disorderly conduct. Some are dealt with by a fine, and sales to children can lead to a review. A solicitor can help with an investigation or prosecution and with any knock on effect on the licence.
What is cumulative impact?

Some councils have adopted a cumulative impact assessment for areas with a high number of licensed premises, often busy town centres. In those areas, new applications and some variations are more likely to be refused if objections are made, unless the applicant can show they will not add to existing problems. A solicitor can tell you whether your premises sits in such an area.
Costs
How much do licensing solicitors charge?

It depends on the type of matter. Routine applications such as transfers, DPS changes and minor variations are often done for a fixed fee. New licences, contested applications, reviews and appeals may be charged hourly or in stages, with a separate fee for attending a hearing. Ask the firm for a written quote before you agree to anything.
How much are council licence fees?

Premises licence fees under the Licensing Act 2003 are set nationally and usually depend on the rateable value of the premises, with an annual fee once granted. Taxi and private hire fees are set locally. All of these change from time to time, so check the current figures with your council or on GOV.UK.
Will I have to pay the council's costs if I lose?

Costs are not usually awarded at a council licensing hearing. On an appeal to the magistrates' court, the court can order one side to pay the other's costs, and councils often ask for theirs if the appeal fails. Your solicitor will explain the likely costs risk before you decide whether to appeal.

Using Leaflegal
Is Leaflegal a law firm?

No. Leaflegal is an introduction service. We do not give legal advice. We pass your enquiry to one regulated law firm that handles licensing work, and any advice you receive comes from that firm. They will look at your situation and explain your options.
Which areas of the country do you cover?

We introduce licensing matters in England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own licensing laws, which work differently, so we do not cover them. If you are unsure whether your matter fits, fill in the form and the firm will tell you if they can help.
How quickly will the firm contact me?

The firm usually gets in touch within one working day, and often sooner. If you have a hearing date, an appeal deadline or a suspension, say so on the form so the firm knows it is urgent. Please give a phone number you can answer.
What information should I give on the form?

A short description is enough. Tell us the type of licence, the council, what you need and any key dates such as an opening date, a completion date or a hearing. You can give the firm documents when they contact you. The more they know at the start, the more useful the first conversation will be.
Do I have to instruct the firm?

No. You are free to decide whether to go ahead after speaking to the firm. There is no obligation and no charge from Leaflegal either way. If you do instruct them, the firm will send you its terms and confirm its fees in writing.
